cse-2014-2-cs-37.approach: Fill the standard LCS dynamic-programming table to get the length $x$, then count the **distinct** subsequences of that length by backtracking through every tie in the table. Finally compute $x + 10y$.

steps.title: Set up the recurrence
steps.body:
$L[i][j]$ = LCS length of the first $i$ symbols of $A$ and the first $j$ of $B$:

$$L[i][j] = \begin{cases} 0 & i=0 \text{ or } j=0 \\ L[i-1][j-1] + 1 & A_i = B_j \\ \max(L[i-1][j],\, L[i][j-1]) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

Row $\varepsilon$ and column $\varepsilon$ are all 0. Row **q**: the first match is $B_2 = q$, so the row becomes $0,0,1,1,1,1,1,1$.

steps.title: Fill rows p and q
steps.body:
Row **p**: $B_1 = p$ gives 1; $B_3 = p$ extends the q at $B_2$: $L[2][3] = L[1][2]+1 = 2$.

Row **q**: $B_2 = q$ after $p$ gives $L[3][2] = 2$; $B_5 = q$ after "qp"/"pq" gives $L[3][5] = L[2][4]+1 = 3$.

steps.title: Fill rows r, r — read off x
steps.body:
Row **r**: $B_4 = r$ gives $L[4][4] = L[3][3]+1 = 3$ and $B_6 = r$ gives $L[4][6] = L[3][5]+1 = 4$.

The second **r** row gives the same values: matching it with $B_6$ yields $L[4][5]+1 = 4$, no improvement.

$x = L[5][7] = 4$.

steps.title: Backtrack every tie to list the distinct LCSs
steps.body:
From $L[5][7]$, follow every way the value 4 can arise (diagonal on a match, up/left on a tie). The distinct strings of length 4 are:

- **qpqr** — q·p·q·r matched at $B$ positions 2, 3, 5, 6
- **qprr** — positions 2, 3, 4, 6
- **pqrr** — positions 1, 2, 4, 6

No other combination reaches 4, so $y = 3$.

cse-2014-2-cs-37.shortcut: A length-4 LCS must end in r (in $A$ only 'qp' precedes its last q, so ending in p or q gives at most 3), and that r must be $B_6$ (before $B_4$ there is only 'pqp'). So count the length-3 common subsequences of $\texttt{qpqr}$ and $\texttt{pqprq}$: qpq, qpr, pqr — three.
pitfalls: Counting backtracking **paths** instead of distinct strings — several paths spell the same subsequence.
Reporting $10x + y = 43$ by swapping the roles of $x$ and $y$.
cse-2014-2-cs-37.verification: Each listed string is a subsequence of both: e.g. pqrr in $\texttt{qpqrr}$ uses positions 2,3,4,5 and in $\texttt{pqprqrp}$ positions 1,2,4,6. A length-5 common subsequence would need all of $A$, but $\texttt{qpqrr}$ is not a subsequence of $B$ (only one r follows the second q).
